Aql: Aquila is the eagle that carried Zeus’s thunderbolts, and in one myth snatched up the youth Ganymede to serve as cupbearer of the gods. You’ll find Ganymede next door as Aquarius. Its brightest star, Altair, is one of our closest naked-eye neighbors at just 17 light-years, and it spins so fast, one turn in about nine hours, that it’s flung into the shape of an egg. Altair anchors the southern corner of the Summer Triangle, right on the Milky Way’s edge.
CMa: Canis Major is Orion’s larger hunting dog, forever at the hunter’s heels across the sky. It carries Sirius, the brightest star in all the night. The ancient Egyptians built their calendar around its dawn return, which foretold the Nile’s flood, and the Romans blamed the sweltering “dog days” on its heat. Sirius is secretly a double, its collapsed white-dwarf companion nicknamed “the Pup.”
Cas: Cassiopeia is the vain queen of myth, punished for boasting she outshone the sea nymphs. The gods bound her to her throne and set it wheeling around the pole, so half the year she hangs upside down. Her five bright stars form an unmistakable W that never sets for most northern viewers. In 1572 a “new star” flared here, a supernova Tycho Brahe studied to help overturn the ancient belief that the heavens never change.
Cru: Crux, the Southern Cross, is the smallest of all 88 constellations and the most famous of the southern sky. It flies on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, and Brazil. The Greeks could see it and counted it as part of Centaurus, never as a cross. Precession then dragged it below the European horizon, and Europeans only charted it again in the age of sail. Right beside it lies the Coalsack, a dark cloud of dust that punches a black hole into the glowing Milky Way.
Cyg: Cygnus is the swan gliding south down the Milky Way, in myth Zeus in disguise, or the grieving friend of Phaethon, who fell from the runaway chariot of the Sun. Its tail-star Deneb is one of the most luminous stars known, its light crossing at least 1,600 light-years to reach us. Aim binoculars at the swan’s head, Albireo, and it splits into a gold-and-blue double star.
Gem: Gemini honors the twins Castor and Pollux, one mortal, one immortal, who loved each other so dearly that when Castor died, Pollux begged Zeus to let them share eternity. The pair were set side by side in the sky, and their two head-stars still shine as a matched pair. Pollux, the brighter, hosts a known planet. Castor looks single but is secretly a knot of six suns bound together.
Leo: Leo is the Nemean lion strangled by Heracles in the first of his twelve labors, its hide impervious to any blade. It’s one of the rare constellations that truly looks the part, a crouching lion whose head and mane are traced by a backward question mark called the Sickle. At its base burns Regulus, “the little king,” a star spinning so fast it’s squashed into an egg, sitting almost exactly on the path the planets follow.
Ori: Orion is the great hunter of Greek myth, set opposite the Scorpion that killed him so the two never share the sky. As Scorpius rises in the east, Orion is already fleeing below the west. His shoulder-star Betelgeuse is a red supergiant near the end of its life. When it finally goes supernova it will briefly blaze bright enough to cast shadows and show in daylight. The fuzzy middle “star” of his sword is the Orion Nebula, a stellar nursery hatching new suns 1,300 light-years away.
Sco: Scorpius is one of the few constellations that genuinely looks like its namesake, a long curving scorpion with a raised, stinging tail. In myth it’s the creature that slew Orion, which is why the gods pinned the two on opposite sides of the sky. Its heart is Antares, a red supergiant whose name means “rival of Mars” for its matching fiery color. Like Betelgeuse, it is living on borrowed time.
Tau: Taurus is the bull Zeus became to carry off the princess Europa, or the beast forever charging the hunter Orion beside it. Its face is the Hyades, the nearest star cluster to Earth, with orange Aldebaran glaring as the bull’s eye. Aldebaran is a foreground interloper, not truly one of the cluster. Ride the bull’s shoulder to the Pleiades, the “Seven Sisters,” a knot of hot blue stars that has drawn human eyes for as long as anyone has watched the sky.
UMa: Ursa Major is the great bear of myth, the nymph Callisto, turned into a bear by a jealous goddess and flung into the sky by her tail. That, the story goes, is why celestial bears have such unnaturally long ones. Her hindquarters form the Big Dipper, the most recognized star pattern in the northern sky. Hidden in the bend of its handle are Mizar and Alcor, a naked-eye double that ancient armies used as a test of good eyesight.
UMi: Ursa Minor is the little bear whose tail-tip is Polaris, the North Star, the one point in the sky that holds nearly still while everything else wheels around it. It won’t keep the honor forever. Earth’s axis slowly wobbles, passing the title from star to star, and in a few thousand years a star in Cepheus will inherit it. The two stars of the bear’s bowl, Kochab and Pherkad, are known as the “Guardians of the Pole.”
And: Andromeda is the chained princess of myth. Her mother Cassiopeia’s boasting so angered the gods that Andromeda was left shackled to a seaside rock as a sacrifice to the monster Cetus, until the hero Perseus swept in to save her. Her constellation cradles the Andromeda Galaxy, the most distant thing most people ever see with the naked eye: a spiral of a trillion stars, 2.5 million light-years away and drifting toward a slow-motion collision with our own Milky Way. To the eye it’s a faint smudge. That smudge is a whole other galaxy.
Aqr: Aquarius, the water-bearer, is usually pictured as the youth Ganymede, carried off by Zeus’s eagle to pour drinks for the gods on Olympus. It’s one of the oldest constellations, long tied to the rainy season by the river peoples who watched for it. Its own stars are faint, but it holds the Helix Nebula, the glowing cast-off shell of a dying star that photographs like a great cosmic eye staring back.
Ari: Aries is the ram of the Golden Fleece, whose golden-wooled hide Jason and the Argonauts sailed the world to claim. Two thousand years ago the Sun crossed into Aries at the start of spring, so “the first point of Aries” still names that moment, even though the slow wobble of Earth’s axis has since slid it into neighboring Pisces. The constellation itself is modest, a small bent line of stars west of the Pleiades.
Aur: Auriga is the charioteer, often the lame Athenian king Erichthonius, who invented the chariot to carry himself. He’s always drawn cradling a goat and her kids. That goat is Capella, the sixth-brightest star in the sky, whose name means “little she-goat”: the mythical Amalthea, whose milk fed the infant Zeus. Golden Capella rides nearly overhead for mid-northern viewers and is in fact a close pair of giant stars.
Boo: Boötes is the herdsman, driving the two bears around the pole through the northern night. He carries Arcturus, the brightest star of the northern sky, a swollen orange giant whose name means “guardian of the bear.” Arcturus is a galactic outsider, plunging through our neighborhood at tremendous speed as part of an ancient stream of stars that doesn’t share the Milky Way’s gentle spin.
Cnc: Cancer is the faintest constellation of the zodiac, so dim that under city lights you may see nothing at all. That suits the crab Hera sent to nip Heracles mid-battle, only to be promptly crushed underfoot. Its redemption is the Beehive Cluster, a puff of light to the naked eye that dissolves into hundreds of sparkling stars in binoculars. The ancients called it Praesepe, “the manger.”
CMi: Canis Minor is Orion’s smaller hunting dog, and it’s really just one bright star with a faint companion. That bright star is Procyon, eighth-brightest in the night, whose name means “before the dog” because it rises just ahead of Sirius, the Dog Star. Procyon is a close neighbor at 11 light-years and, like Sirius, drags a dead white-dwarf companion around with it. The two dog-stars and Betelgeuse form the Winter Triangle.
Cap: Capricornus is the strange sea-goat, a goat with a fish’s tail, born when the god Pan leapt into a river to flee a monster and his submerged half turned piscine. It’s one of the oldest and faintest signs of the zodiac, shaped like a wide arrowhead or a lopsided grin. The Tropic of Capricorn still carries its name from an age when the Sun stood here at the southern solstice, though precession has since carried that point into Sagittarius.
Cen: Centaurus is the wise centaur, often Chiron, tutor of heroes, and it holds the closest stars to our Sun. Alpha Centauri is a bright triple system just 4.4 light-years away, and its faint red member Proxima is the nearest star of all. Centaurus also cradles Omega Centauri, the largest globular cluster in the sky, a swarm of millions of ancient stars that may be the stripped-down heart of a devoured galaxy. From the far south it’s brilliant. Northern viewers glimpse only its top.
Cep: Cepheus is the king, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda, drawn as a faint house-shape near the pole. Its quiet stars hide two giants of astronomy: the Garnet Star, one of the largest and reddest stars known, and Delta Cephei, the prototype of the “Cepheid” variables. Because a Cepheid’s steady pulse reveals its true brightness, these stars became the yardstick that first let astronomers measure the distance to other galaxies.
CrB: Corona Borealis is an arc of seven stars, the jeweled crown of the princess Ariadne, flung into the heavens by the god Dionysus as a wedding gift. Tucked within it is the “Blaze Star,” a dim system that erupts as a nova roughly once a human lifetime, briefly flaring into naked-eye view before fading back to obscurity. Most nights the little crown is a quiet semicircle just east of Boötes.
Crv: Corvus is the crow of Apollo, sent to fetch water in a cup but dallying to wait for figs to ripen, then lying about the delay and blaming a water-snake. Apollo saw through it and flung crow, cup, and snake into the sky as Corvus, Crater, and Hydra, cursing the crow to eternal thirst just out of reach of the cup. Its four stars make a small, crisp sail-shape southwest of bright Spica.
Del: Delphinus is the dolphin that talked the sea-nymph Amphitrite into marrying Poseidon, and in another tale the one that carried the drowning poet Arion safely to shore. It’s a tiny diamond of stars set in a lonely patch of sky, which only makes it stand out more. Two of its stars carry the odd names Sualocin and Rotanev. Spell them backwards and you get Nicolaus Venator, an astronomer who slyly smuggled his own name into the stars.
Dra: Draco is the dragon, Ladon, the hundred-headed guardian of the golden apples slain by Heracles, coiling its long body around the north pole between the two bears. Around 2700 BC its star Thuban, not Polaris, was the North Star, and the Egyptians aligned the Great Pyramid to it. The slow wobble of Earth’s axis will make Thuban the pole star once again in another 20,000 years.
Eri: Eridanus is the great celestial river, into which the boy Phaethon crashed after losing control of the Sun’s chariot and scorching the Earth. It’s one of the longest constellations, meandering from near Orion’s foot all the way down into the far southern sky. Its end is marked by Achernar, literally “the river’s end,” which spins so ferociously that it’s the flattest star known, its equator bulging more than 50% wider than the distance from pole to pole.
Her: Hercules is the kneeling strongman of the sky, marked by the Keystone, a lopsided box of four stars forming his torso. Clinging to that box is M13, the finest globular cluster in the north, a city of hundreds of thousands of stars and the target of the 1974 Arecibo message, humanity’s first deliberate radio note aimed at the stars. By chance, this is also the patch of sky our whole Solar System is drifting toward as it orbits the galaxy.
Hya: Hydra is the many-headed water-serpent that grew two heads for every one Heracles struck off, until he seared each stump with fire. It’s the largest constellation in the sky, sprawling more than a quarter of the way around the heavens. Despite that reach it’s mostly faint, with a single bright star: Alphard, “the solitary one,” glowing alone in an empty stretch of sky. It takes hours to fully rise, its tail still climbing as its head sets.
Lep: Lepus is the hare crouching right beneath Orion’s feet, forever fleeing the hunter and his two dogs. It’s an old and quiet constellation, easy to overlook, but it hides one gem: Hind’s Crimson Star, a carbon star so deeply red it’s been likened to a glowing coal or a drop of blood among the stars. Its color comes from soot in the star’s outer layers, which filters away the blue light.
Lib: Libra, the scales, is the only zodiac constellation that’s an object rather than a living thing, the balance of justice held by the neighboring maiden Virgo. It wasn’t always its own. The Romans split it from Scorpius, which is why its brightest stars are still named Zubenelgenubi and Zubeneschamali, the “southern claw” and “northern claw.” In an earlier age the Sun crossed Libra at the autumn equinox, when day and night hang in perfect balance.
Lyr: Lyra is the lyre of Orpheus, the musician whose playing was so beautiful it charmed stones and nearly won his wife back from the dead. Its jewel is Vega, the fifth-brightest star, which was the North Star some 14,000 years ago and will be again, and which astronomers long used as the very definition of brightness “zero.” Vega was also the first star ever photographed. Near it hangs the Ring Nebula, a dying star’s smoke-ring you can catch in a small telescope.
Oph: Ophiuchus is the serpent-bearer, the great healer Asclepius, so skilled he could raise the dead until Zeus struck him down with a thunderbolt to protect the natural order and set him among the stars. The Sun actually passes through Ophiuchus each year, making it the sky’s unofficial “thirteenth” zodiac sign that horoscopes leave out. It also hosts Barnard’s Star, a dim red dwarf that races across our sky faster than any other star.
Peg: Pegasus is the winged horse, sprung from the blood of the slain Gorgon Medusa and tamed to carry heroes and the thunderbolts of Zeus. Four stars mark the Great Square of Pegasus, a giant, nearly-empty box that dominates its stretch of sky. One of its stars, 51 Pegasi, made history in 1995 as the first Sun-like star found to host a planet, a discovery that opened the age of exoplanets and later won a Nobel Prize.
Per: Perseus is the hero who beheaded Medusa and rescued Andromeda from the sea-monster, and he still holds the Gorgon’s severed head, marked by the star Algol. Algol is the “Demon Star”: every 2.9 days a dim companion eclipses it and you can watch it visibly fade and rebrighten, an old omen of misfortune that turned out to be clockwork. Each August the Perseid meteor shower rains down from this corner of the sky.
Psc: Pisces is the pair of fish, Aphrodite and her son Eros, who leapt into a river and turned to fish to escape the fire-monster Typhon, tying their tails together so they’d never be separated. It’s a faint, watery constellation, best known today for holding the vernal equinox. The point where the Sun crosses the equator each spring has slowly drifted into Pisces over the ages. A small ring of stars called the Circlet marks the head of one fish.
PsA: Piscis Austrinus, the southern fish, is drawn drinking the stream poured out by Aquarius above it, and in myth is the parent of the two zodiac fish. It has a single claim to fame: Fomalhaut, the “Lonely Star of Autumn,” which shines by itself in an otherwise empty stretch of the southern sky. Fomalhaut is girdled by a vast ring of dust and debris, a solar system still under construction, that astronomers have photographed directly.
Pup: Puppis is the stern of Argo Navis, the ship that carried Jason and the Argonauts after the Golden Fleece, a constellation once so enormous that the astronomer Lacaille broke it into three. Its brightest star, Naos, is a rare blue supergiant, one of the hottest stars visible to the eye, blazing hundreds of thousands of times brighter than the Sun. It’s also a “runaway,” flung across the galaxy by some ancient stellar catastrophe.
Sgr: Sagittarius is the archer, a centaur drawing his bow straight at the heart of the neighboring Scorpion. Its brightest stars form the Teapot, and the “steam” rising from its spout is the glowing central bulge of our own Milky Way. Look here and you’re gazing toward the very center of the galaxy, where a supermassive black hole four million times the mass of the Sun lies hidden behind the star clouds.
Ser: Serpens is the great snake wrestled by the serpent-bearer Ophiuchus, and it’s the only constellation broken into two separate pieces, a head to the west and a tail to the east, with the healer standing between them. In its tail lies the Eagle Nebula, home of the “Pillars of Creation,” towering columns of gas where new stars are being born. The Hubble telescope’s image of them is one of the most famous ever taken.
Vel: Vela is the sails of Argo Navis, the Argonauts’ ship, another of the three pieces Lacaille carved from that ancient vessel. Hidden within it is the Vela supernova remnant, the shredded wreckage of a star that exploded about 11,000 years ago, close enough that our ancestors may have seen it blaze, with a spinning neutron star at its core. Several of its stars also form the “False Cross,” which fools southern navigators into mistaking it for the true Southern Cross.
Vir: Virgo is the maiden, often Astraea, goddess of justice, or Demeter of the harvest, holding an ear of wheat marked by the bright blue star Spica. It’s the second-largest constellation and a deep window on the universe. It holds the Virgo Cluster of over a thousand galaxies, and the galaxy M87, whose central black hole became the first ever photographed, in 2019. Spica itself is a pair of scorching stars whipping around each other every four days.
Ant: Antlia, the air pump, is one of the faint southern constellations invented in the 1750s by the astronomer Lacaille, who filled the far-southern sky with the instruments of science and art rather than gods and heroes. It honors the vacuum air pump, a cutting-edge laboratory device of the Enlightenment. There’s little to see here with the naked eye, just a dim scatter of stars in a quiet patch below Hydra.
Aps: Apus is the bird of paradise, one of a dozen exotic-animal constellations mapped by Dutch navigators sailing the southern seas in the 1590s. Its name comes from a Greek word meaning “without feet.” Early bird-of-paradise skins reached Europe with the legs removed, sparking a legend that the birds floated endlessly on the wind and never landed. It sits faint and obscure near the south celestial pole.
Ara: Ara is the altar, and an ancient one: this is the altar on which the gods of Olympus swore their alliance before making war on the Titans, its rising smoke said to have formed the Milky Way. It sits in the southern Milky Way just below the tail of Scorpius, in a rich field of stars. Faint to northern eyes, from the south it stands in one of the most star-strewn regions of the sky.
Cae: Caelum, the engraver’s chisel, is one of the smallest and faintest constellations in the entire sky, a near-empty sliver invented by Lacaille to fill a gap in the far south. It has no bright stars, no famous objects, and no mythology. It’s essentially a placeholder honoring a sculptor’s tool. If you can pick it out at all under dark skies, you’ve earned it.
Cam: Camelopardalis is the giraffe. Its tongue-twisting name comes from the Greek for “camel-leopard,” since the ancients saw the long-necked, spotted animal as a blend of the two. It’s a large constellation sprawling across the far north near the pole, yet so faint that no one bothered to chart it until the 1600s. There are almost no bright stars here. It’s a great blank stretch that most people look straight past.
CVn: Canes Venatici, the hunting dogs, are the two hounds held on a leash by the herdsman Boötes as he chases the great bear around the pole, invented by the astronomer Hevelius to tidy up a gap of faint stars. Its glory lies far beyond those stars, in the Whirlpool Galaxy, a face-on spiral locked in a slow collision with a smaller companion. It was in the Whirlpool that astronomers first recognized the spiral shape of a “nebula.”
Car: Carina is the keel of Argo Navis, the great ship of Jason’s Argonauts, and the richest of the three pieces Lacaille split it into. It carries Canopus, the second-brightest star in the entire night sky, long used by spacecraft as a navigation beacon. It also holds the vast Carina Nebula and the unstable star Eta Carinae, which in the 1840s flared into a “Great Eruption,” briefly becoming one of the sky’s brightest stars before nearly tearing itself apart.
Cet: Cetus is the sea-monster sent to devour Andromeda before Perseus turned it to stone, a sprawling beast of a constellation befitting its name. It holds a wonder: Mira, “the Amazing,” the first star ever found to pulse, swelling and fading over eleven months from easy naked-eye brightness to invisibility and back. Mira is a dying red giant, shedding its outer layers and trailing a comet-like tail light-years long.
Cha: Chamaeleon, the chameleon, is a small, dim constellation huddled near the south celestial pole, one of the southern-sky animals named by Dutch seafarers around 1600. In a fitting bit of celestial wit, the little chameleon lies not far from Musca, the fly, as if forever about to catch it. Its faint stars and dark dust clouds shelter a nursery of newborn stars visible only to telescopes.
Cir: Circinus is the drafting compass, the twin-legged tool for drawing circles, another of Lacaille’s instruments of science tucked into the southern sky. It’s a tiny, faint constellation squeezed right beside the brilliant pointer stars Alpha and Beta Centauri, which tend to steal all the attention. It sits in a rich but easily overlooked stretch of the southern Milky Way.
Col: Columba is the dove, added to the sky around 1600 to represent either the dove Noah released from the ark or the one the Argonauts sent ahead to guide their ship through the clashing rocks. It sits just south of the brilliant Dog Star region, a quiet gathering of modest stars. One of them, Mu Columbae, is a “runaway” flung out of the Orion Nebula millions of years ago and still fleeing across the galaxy.
Com: Coma Berenices is one of the few constellations named for a real person: Queen Berenice of Egypt, who cut off her famous hair as an offering for her husband’s safe return from war. When it vanished from the temple, the court astronomer declared the gods had set it in the sky. The “hair” is a genuine loose cluster of stars you can see shimmering on a dark night. Just beyond it lies a deep window out of our galaxy, crowded with distant clusters of galaxies.
CrA: Corona Australis is the southern crown, a little arc of stars mirroring the better-known northern crown across the sky. It’s sometimes cast as a wreath laid at the feet of the neighboring archer, Sagittarius. Faint but neat, it curls beside the Milky Way and shelters a dark cloud where new stars are quietly being born.
Crt: Crater is the cup, the goblet of Apollo, and it shares a story with its neighbors Corvus and Hydra. The crow sent to fill it dawdled, then lied, and all three were cast into the sky, the thirsty crow kept forever from drinking. It’s a small, faint arc of stars shaped convincingly like a two-handled chalice. There’s little that’s bright here, but the tidy goblet pattern is a satisfying find under dark skies.
Dor: Dorado is the dolphinfish, one of the southern-sea creatures charted by Dutch navigators, but its real treasure isn’t a star at all. It holds most of the Large Magellanic Cloud, an entire satellite galaxy orbiting our Milky Way, visible from the south as a detached patch of soft light. Within it glows the Tarantula Nebula, a star-forming region so enormous that if it sat where the Orion Nebula does, it would cast shadows on Earth.
Equ: Equuleus, the little horse, is the second-smallest constellation in the sky, just a faint knot of stars representing the foal Celeris, a companion of the winged Pegasus beside it. It’s so dim and modest it’s easy to miss entirely. With no bright stars and no showpiece objects, its whole charm is being the sky’s tiny, overlooked pony.
For: Fornax is the furnace, originally the “chemical furnace,” one of Lacaille’s tributes to science, honoring the furnace of the new chemistry taking shape in Enlightenment laboratories. Its faint stars hide real depth. This is a favorite hunting ground for astronomers, home to the Fornax cluster of galaxies and a small dwarf galaxy orbiting our own. Some of the deepest images ever taken of the distant universe peer straight out through this quiet window.
Gru: Grus is the crane, a long-necked wading bird set among the southern constellations by Dutch explorers around 1600, and its stars were once considered the tail of neighboring Piscis Austrinus. Across several cultures the same stars were seen as a bird, which feels apt. Its brightest star, Alnair, shines a clean blue-white, riding high for southern viewers and barely clearing the horizon for northern ones.
Hor: Horologium, the pendulum clock, is another of Lacaille’s scientific instruments, a nod to the precision timekeeping that made accurate astronomy possible. It’s a long, faint, winding trickle of stars in the southern sky with little to catch the eye. Its shape is thin and unremarkable, ticking quietly away below the celestial equator.
Hyi: Hydrus is the little water-snake, not to be confused with the huge Hydra of the north, one of the southern serpents mapped by Dutch navigators near the south pole. It winds modestly between the two Magellanic Clouds, as if slithering from one to the other. Its stars are faint, but it marks a memorable corner of the deep southern sky.
Ind: Indus represents an Indian, a figure meant to depict the native peoples the Dutch encountered on their voyages of the 1590s, drawn holding spears among the southern stars. It’s a faint, sprawling constellation with no bright showpieces. One of its stars, Epsilon Indi, is a near neighbor of the Sun and an early target in the search for nearby planets and life.
Lac: Lacerta, the lizard, is a small zigzag of faint stars squeezed into a gap between Cygnus and Andromeda, invented by the astronomer Hevelius, who slipped a little reptile into a crevice too cramped for anything grander. Its W-shape is a fainter echo of nearby Cassiopeia. There’s not much bright to see, but it lies in a pretty stretch of the Milky Way.
LMi: Leo Minor, the little lion, is a scrap of faint stars the astronomer Hevelius tucked between the Great Bear and the big Lion in the 1600s. It has no mythology and no bright stars, just a small, quiet triangle few people ever notice. It carries the modest distinction of being one of the sky’s most anonymous constellations, overshadowed by grander neighbors on every side.
Lup: Lupus is the wolf, though to the ancient Greeks it was simply “the beast,” a wild animal impaled on the spear of the neighboring centaur, Centaurus, as an offering. Only later did it become specifically a wolf. It sits in a rich southern stretch of the Milky Way and once hosted the most brilliant supernova in recorded history, seen around the world in the year 1006, bright enough to read by at night.
Lyn: Lynx is a faint, meandering trail of stars the astronomer Hevelius named with a joke: he claimed you’d need the sharp eyes of a lynx to see it at all. It fills a large, dim gap between the Great Bear and Auriga with almost nothing bright. Its whole personality is its own faintness, a wry monument to observing under dark skies.
Men: Mensa, the table, is the faintest constellation in the entire sky. Not one of its stars reaches even the brightness of the dimmest stars in the Big Dipper. It’s also the only constellation named for a real place on Earth: Table Mountain in South Africa, where Lacaille sat charting the southern sky. Part of the Large Magellanic Cloud drifts across it like the “tablecloth” of cloud that famously drapes the real mountain.
Mic: Microscopium, the microscope, is one of Lacaille’s Enlightenment instruments, celebrating the device that opened up the world of the very small just as the telescope opened the very large. It’s a faint, unremarkable square of dim stars south of Capricornus. There’s essentially nothing here for the naked eye, a quiet tribute to a great invention.
Mon: Monoceros is the unicorn, a faint constellation added around 1600 in what looks like a dark gap. It isn’t dark at all, because the Milky Way runs right through it. Its dim stars hide the Rosette Nebula, a great flower of glowing gas with a star cluster at its heart, and the sparkling Christmas Tree Cluster. It sits smack in the middle of the bright Winter Triangle, ringed by Sirius, Betelgeuse, and Procyon.
Mus: Musca is the fly, the only insect among the 88 constellations, first charted by Dutch navigators near the south pole. They called it simply the fly, but Bayer misread the Dutch and labeled it Apis, the bee, a mistake that stuck for 150 years until Lacaille put the fly back. It buzzes appropriately close to Chamaeleon, the chameleon that might just snap it up. Small and faint but set in the southern Milky Way, it hosts a couple of fine globular clusters and a dark nebula for telescope users.
Nor: Norma is the carpenter’s square, a right-angled level and rule, another of Lacaille’s workshop tools raised into the southern sky. Oddly, it has no stars labeled alpha or beta. When the modern constellation boundaries were fixed in 1930, its two brightest were left just inside neighboring Scorpius. It lies in a dense, dust-strewn band of the Milky Way, and a whole spiral arm of our galaxy is named the Norma Arm for the direction it lies in.
Oct: Octans, the octant, is the navigator’s angle-measuring instrument, and Lacaille gave it pride of place, for it contains the south celestial pole, the fixed pivot of the entire southern sky. But the far south has no bright pole star. Its stand-in, Sigma Octantis, is so dim it’s barely visible, leaving southern sailors without an easy “South Star” the way the north has Polaris. The whole sky wheels silently around this faint, empty point.
Pav: Pavo is the peacock, one of the southern birds named by Dutch explorers. In myth the peacock is sacred to the goddess Hera, whose watchman Argus had his hundred eyes set into its tail. Its brightest star is simply named Peacock, one of the few stars to carry its own constellation’s nickname. It shines blue-white in the deep southern sky.
Phe: Phoenix is the immortal firebird that burns to ash and is reborn, a fitting emblem the Dutch navigators set in the southern sky, since the same myth of a self-resurrecting bird appears in cultures across the ancient world. It’s a modest constellation whose brightest star, Ankaa, glows quietly at its heart. Every so often its dim reaches host a flurry of shooting stars, the Phoenicids, streaming from the reborn bird.
Pic: Pictor, the painter’s easel, is a faint southern constellation from Lacaille’s studio of instruments, but it holds one of the most important stars in modern astronomy. Beta Pictoris is a young star wrapped in a vast disk of dust and debris, the first such disk ever imaged, where planets are actively forming. Astronomers have even photographed a giant planet taking shape within it. It’s a whole solar system caught in the act of being born.
Pyx: Pyxis is the mariner’s compass, the magnetic needle that guided ships, placed by Lacaille near the great celestial vessel Argo Navis as if the ship’s compass had been set beside its keel and sails. It’s a small, faint constellation with little to show the naked eye. Its chief curiosity is a recurrent nova, a star that has flared into view several times over the past century and gone quiet again.
Ret: Reticulum, the reticle, honors the fine crosshair grid Lacaille placed in his telescope eyepiece to measure star positions with precision, in a sense the very tool that let him map the constellations around it. It’s a small, faint diamond of stars in the deep southern sky. A quiet monument to careful measurement, it holds little else to catch the casual eye.
Sge: Sagitta is the arrow, the third-smallest constellation in the sky, and despite its faintness it’s an ancient one, seen variously as the arrow of Heracles, of Apollo, or the shaft Eros used to kindle love. It flies between the eagle Aquila and the swan Cygnus, a tiny dart against the Milky Way. Small as it is, its neat arrow shape is genuinely convincing once you find it.
Scl: Sculptor, the sculptor’s studio, is a faint southern constellation from Lacaille’s artistic workshop, but it looks out on something grand. It contains the south pole of our own galaxy, the direction of least obscuring dust, giving a clear view into deep space. Through this window lie the bright Sculptor Galaxy and a nearby group of galaxies. There’s little bright in the foreground, but the depths beyond are spectacular.
Sct: Scutum is the shield, specifically the shield of the Polish king John III Sobieski, honored by the astronomer Hevelius after the king’s victory turned back the siege of Vienna. Small and faint, it nonetheless sits atop the Scutum Star Cloud, one of the brightest, densest patches of the whole Milky Way. Sweep it with binoculars to find the Wild Duck Cluster, a glittering swarm shaped like ducks in flight.
Sex: Sextans is the sextant, named by the astronomer Hevelius for the great angle-measuring instrument he used to catalog the stars, the very one lost when his observatory burned down in 1679. He placed the faint little constellation beneath Leo as a memorial to it. There’s almost nothing bright here, but hidden in its dimness is the Spindle Galaxy, a sleek edge-on disk for telescope users.
Tel: Telescopium, the telescope, is Lacaille’s tribute to the instrument that transformed astronomy, apt since his own southern survey was made possible by it. It’s a faint, unassuming constellation just south of Sagittarius, with little to draw the naked eye. Like many of Lacaille’s instruments, its charm is conceptual, a quiet salute to the tool that let humanity see the sky anew.
Tri: Triangulum is simply a triangle, three stars forming a slim, distinct wedge, yet this modest shape was recognized as its own constellation even by the ancient Greeks. Its fame lies in the Triangulum Galaxy, the third-largest member of our Local Group of galaxies. Under truly dark skies it is, alongside the Andromeda Galaxy, one of the most distant objects visible to the unaided human eye, nearly three million light-years away.
TrA: Triangulum Australe, the southern triangle, is a small but bright and genuinely triangular constellation charted by Dutch navigators, clearer and more compact than its fainter northern namesake. Its three main stars make a neat, easy shape in the far-southern Milky Way. Tucked beside it lie fine star clusters, making its rich patch of sky a rewarding sweep with binoculars.
Tuc: Tucana is the toucan, one of the southern birds named by Dutch navigators, and like its neighbors it hides a galaxy. It holds the Small Magellanic Cloud, a companion galaxy to the Milky Way visible as a soft patch of light from the south. Right beside it glitters 47 Tucanae, one of the finest globular clusters in the entire sky, a tight ball of up to a million stars, bright enough to spot with the naked eye.
Vol: Volans is the flying fish, one of the southern-sea creatures charted by Dutch sailors who would have watched real flying fish skim the waves on their voyages. The little fish appears to leap right beside the great ship Carina. Faint and far south with no bright stars, it hides the Meathook Galaxy, a spiral dramatically bent into a hook by a past gravitational encounter.
Vul: Vulpecula, the little fox, is a faint constellation the astronomer Hevelius first drew as a fox carrying a goose in its jaws. Its dim stars hide a big place in history. Here lies the Dumbbell Nebula, the first planetary nebula ever discovered, and it was in Vulpecula that astronomers detected the very first pulsar in 1967, a spinning dead star whose pulses were so eerily regular they were half-jokingly labeled “LGM,” for Little Green Men.
